title: Throughput sync: per-customer shard weights & soft token quotas
summary: SE-led deep-dive on throughput controls: discussed per-customer shard weighting, soft token quotas, and how to tune max_num_seqs with continuous batching. Covered KV-cache prewarm strategies for VPC/on-prem, quantization trade-offs for tail latency, and an experiment plan to run sustained 90th/99th percentile latency benches. Agreed on follow-ups: benchmark script, security doc link, and a 2-week pilot with shard-weighting enabled.

transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-08-19
Start: 14:30 UTC
Duration: ~52 minutes
Attendees: Lena Ortiz (Redwood AE), Marcus Li (Redwood SE), Priya Shah (Viant - Platform Eng), Tom Reilly (Viant - SRE), Markus Engel (Viant - CTO)

Summary (auto): Quick goals: get per-tenant fairness while preserving cluster throughput; try soft token quotas to avoid hard throttling; prove max_num_seqs settings under realistic seq mix.

Topics: continuous batching / scheduler knobs / max_num_seqs / shard weights / soft token quotas / kv prewarm / quantization tradeoffs / VPC networking

--- Transcript ---
[00:00] Lena Ortiz: hey everyone, thanks for joining, I think we have about 50 minutes, we wanted to focus on throughput controls — specifically per-customer shard weighting and the softer token quota approach that folks have been testing. Marcus is going to run through the perf knob matrix, then we can map that to your traffic.
[00:22] Marcus Li: hey, yeah hi. quick note: i'll try to keep this practical, we know Viant has mixed seqs — a lot of short queries plus longer context generations. so, the two levers we see most impact from are max_num_seqs and the token ceiling / soft quota. combined with continuous batching these let you smooth tails without killing throughput.
[00:45] Priya Shah: thanks. to be clear, our main worry is that one tenant (internal analytics) occasionally spikes and causes upstream latency spikes for product traffic — we have a VPC and on-prem plans so we need isolation but not total waste of capacity.
[01:02] Marcus Li: totally, that's exactly where shard weights help. instead of absolute pinning to a GPU pool, we compute per-tenant weights that bias the scheduler. so tenant A gets 30% of slots on average, tenant B 10%, etc. weight is soft — it doesn't block others completely during low load.
[01:22] Markus Engel: is that weight enforced by max_num_seqs or by token accounting? like, can a tenant consume a bunch of short seqs and starve a long-seq tenant?
[01:35] Marcus Li: good question. we use a two-tier accounting: slot allocation primarily governed by max_num_seqs (roughly sequences allowed concurrently) and token accounting to limit token-rate. short seqs consume fewer tokens but still take a slot while generating; so you can end up with slot contention. we mitigate with priority weights and an adaptive slot reclamation strategy — if a tenant is hitting token quota but holding slots with tiny token progress, the governor will preempt or deprioritize their new batch windows.
[02:03] Tom Reilly: preempt how? interrupts running in the mid-sequence? that's not great for model state.
[02:12] Marcus Li: right, we don't kill in-flight tokens. preemption is applied at batching boundaries or when scheduling new windows; we let in-flight sequences finish. we can also enable soft token throttles where responses get a low-priority flag and are placed into a longer-latency pathway that uses cheaper model variants or quantized backends.
[02:33] Priya Shah: when you say cheaper model variants, do you mean fallback to a smaller model or quantized int4 version?
[02:40] Marcus Li: both are options. in many cases, int8 or int4 variants reduce tail latency by reducing memory bandwidth, but quality can drift. we recommend running quality checks on a band of prompts. for critical product traffic you'd pin to a higher-quality variant and only soft-fallback to int4 for non-critical analytic jobs.
[02:58] Lena Ortiz: quick product note — console shows per-route cost and latency. we'll add the shard-weight view to the tenancy page so you can see per-tenant slot usage and token burn live.
[03:12] [00:03:14] Markus Engel: what's the baseline max_num_seqs you'd recommend for our workload? our sample data: median seq length 18 tokens, ~5% > 512 tokens.
[03:28] Marcus Li: with your median and that tail a conservative starting point is max_num_seqs = 256 per GPU for mixed workloads on A100-like hardware; for continuous batching we often push to 384-512 if KV hit-rate is high and token mix is small. but the trade-off: increasing max_num_seqs increases windowing for batching which helps throughput but can raise p99 if KV hit-rate drops. so KV prewarm is critical.
[03:56] Priya Shah: can you explain the KV prewarm pattern you recommend? we have a cold-start problem after deploys.
[04:04] Marcus Li: sure — two strategies: active prewarm (replay representative prefixes through the cluster before traffic hits) and passive prewarm (maintain a hot set by synthetic short probes). for on-prem/VPC you can run a small prewarm job at deploy time; for hosted we can automate with a webhook. the aim is to raise kv hit-rate above ~70% for typical prompt prefixes.
[04:27] Tom Reilly: how much does KV hit-rate correlate with CPU/GPU utilization? we've seen GPU stalls because KV misses cause disk reads.
[04:34] Marcus Li: KV misses increase latency because the runtime must recompute cache entries and there's more memory traffic — GPU utilization can actually go down while token-latency spikes, because the pipeline stalls. That's why batching windows and slot counts must be tuned together.
[04:52] [00:05:00] Priya Shah: ok, you mentioned soft token quotas — can you walk through an example under a burst?
[05:03] Marcus Li: example: tenant X has soft quota 10k tokens/min and weight 20%. first 10k tokens are normal. when they bump beyond that in a spike, rather than hard-refuse we mark their requests as soft-throttled: they remain in the queue but are scheduled behind non-throttled tenants. additionally, we can route them to a quantized path or smaller model. the idea is graceful degradation: throughput is preserved for priority tenants while spikes get lower priority but not 503s.
[05:32] Markus Engel: does that require client-side retry logic? we don't want to push complexity to clients.
[05:38] Marcus Li: generally no. for soft-throttled requests you still get responses, just slower. we do surface headers that explain the degradation (x-redwood-soft-throttle: true) so you can instrument SLAs. if you want client retries, that's optional — but not required.
[05:54] [00:06:00] Tom Reilly: curious about continuous batching -- we've got a strict p95 latency SLA for product traffic (<= 200ms). can continuous batching coexist with tight SLAs?
[06:07] Marcus Li: yes — continuous batching is workload-aware: we prioritize low-latency routes and reduce their windowing. for your product route you'd lower max_num_seqs or enable priority windows so that product requests see minimal batching delay. Meanwhile background analytics can be packed aggressively. it's a balance: smaller windows reduce throughput efficiency but improve latency.
[06:29] Priya Shah: can we do per-route max_num_seqs?
[06:33] Marcus Li: we support per-route configs — route-level target_num_seqs and tenant-level shard weights combine in the scheduler to produce effective allocation. that's how you get the product route low-latency while keeping analytics cost-effective.
[06:44] [00:06:45] Lena Ortiz: quick interruption — Markus, do you have any specific tail issues you saw in the last incident?
[06:51] Markus Engel: yes, last month during a data export our p99 jumped 3x; postmortem shows many KV misses and a single analytics job dominated slots because it opened a ton of short seq requests.
[07:05] Marcus Li: yep that's the classic short-seq attack on slots. that's where adaptive slot reclamation + token quotas are effective: we detect high slot occupancy with low token progress and shift those requests to be lower priority or place them on different shards.
[07:20] [00:07:30] Priya Shah: how do you recommend we tune token ceilings — absolute numbers or percent of capacity?
[07:36] Marcus Li: we typically start with percent of expected sustained capacity (e.g., 20-30% per large tenant) and then refine with benches. soft quotas are best tuned via synthetic bursts: push 3x normal traffic for 5 minutes and watch degradation curves.
[07:50] Tom Reilly: any tips for VPC/on-prem network variability? we tend to see higher tail due to egress bandwidth constraints between control plane and nodes.
[07:59] Marcus Li: for VPC/on-prem, keep control-plane to data-plane hops minimal; prefer colocated KV stores where possible. also set conservative windowing and increase prefetch margin. we can provide a config template: reduce max_num_seqs by ~20% from hosted defaults, increase retry/backoff thresholds, and use explicit KV prewarm at deploy.
[08:23] [00:08:30] Lena Ortiz: Marcus, can you walk through the experiment plan you proposed?
[08:29] Marcus Li: sure. steps: 1) run bench script that simulates your historical distribution (short vs long seqs) and ramps to 12k RPS, capture p50/p90/p99 token latencies, slot occupancy, kv hit-rate. 2) toggle shard-weighting on/off and observe fairness vs cluster throughput. 3) enable soft token quotas and measure graceful degradation. 4) test quantized fallback (int8/int4) on background traffic and run kalite checks for quality.
[09:02] Priya Shah: for quantized fallback, can we capture side-by-side output diffs? we need to check hallucination rates and prompt completions.
[09:09] Marcus Li: yes we'll produce a small eval harness that runs your prompt-set against both variants and emits a quality delta report.
[09:16] [00:09:20] Markus Engel: any caveats about hardware topology — NUMA, interconnect — that we should know when configuring max_num_seqs?
[09:26] Marcus Li: yes: for multi-socket setups or MIG-like partitions, you need to align slot counts with actual device memory and communication patterns. a per-device max_num_seqs is more predictable than a flat-per-node number. also watch for host-side mem bandwidth — that's a common hidden bottleneck.
[09:44] Tom Reilly: what's the expected cost delta if we enable more aggressive batching vs keeping low windows for product?
[09:51] Marcus Li: aggressive batching often reduces per-token cost by 15-30% depending on model and kv hit-rate; but if you need to lower windows for latency you may lose some of that. that's why per-route configs give you the best of both: product stays low-latency, analytics batched aggressively. we can simulate cost in the bench results.
[10:08] [00:10:15] Pria Shah: small nit — you mentioned headers for soft-throttle, is there a console metric we can alert on?
[10:22] Marcus Li: yes console surfaces soft-throttle rate per tenant and the token burn rate. set alerts on soft-throttle > 5% sustained.
[10:29] [00:10:35] Lena Ortiz: ok let's go into a short Q/A — any other specific asks from Viant?
[10:40] Priya Shah: can we get a recommended default config file for on-prem? we don't want to make naive mistakes.
[10:47] Marcus Li: yes we'll attach a template: includes per-device max_num_seqs, initial shard-weight suggestions, prewarm script, and recommended soft-quota percentages.
[10:56] Markus Engel: curious whether model compilation (kernel selection) interacts with quantized fallbacks — do you need separate compiled kernels for int4?
[11:06] Marcus Li: yes different kernels and often different memory layouts. compiling ahead for your target hardware is important — that's why the bench includes a compile step to pick the best kernels.
[11:16] [00:11:30] Tom Reilly: are there any known issues with eviction policies in the KV store that might cause oscillation with soft quotas?
[11:25] Marcus Li: if eviction is too aggressive, KV hit-rate collapses and the scheduler sees higher latency and increases windows, which makes eviction worse — a positive feedback loop. we solve this with eviction hysteresis and prefetch thresholds so we don't thrash.
[11:41] [00:11:50] Priya Shah: what's a safe starting soft quota number for a tenant that bursts occasionally?
[11:56] Marcus Li: try 2x your average token-per-minute for short experiments, or a percent of cluster capacity (e.g., 10-20%). use the bench to find the knee.
[12:08] [00:12:10] Lena Ortiz: ok, time check — we have about 40 minutes left, Marcus do you want to demo the bench harness briefly?
[12:18] Marcus Li: sure, i'll share my screen — (screen share) this harness is a simple k6 + custom token generator; you can drive seq-length distribution, route weights, and ramp patterns. here are example slides: https://redwood.ai/bench-examples (link shared).
[12:38] [00:12:40] Priya Shah: link looked like internal redwood; will you share a fork for Viant?
[12:45] Marcus Li: yes i'll share a repo and a runnable docker. also attach a JSON traffic profile we created from a small sample you sent earlier.
[12:52] Markus Engel: when we flip shard weighting, how quickly does the scheduler adapt? minutes? seconds?
[12:59] Marcus Li: it depends on your autoscale and sampling window; by default weights apply per scheduling epoch (few seconds) and settle in 30-90 seconds. without autoscale it's mainly a scheduler effect; with autoscale it can be a few minutes.
[13:15] [00:13:20] Tom Reilly: any special logging we should enable to troubleshoot slot contention?
[13:22] Marcus Li: enable per-slot occupancy logs and the token-progress tracer. those give you which tenant holds which slot and its advancing token pointer. we can turn those on for a short window because they are high-volume.
[13:36] [00:13:40] Priya Shah: question on fallback: do you do reranking or quality checks after quantized fallback? we don't want bad completions surfaced.
[13:48] Marcus Li: for high-risk routes we recommend an output-eval step for fallback responses: run a lightweight classifier or reranker to detect glaring regressions before returning; that adds a bit of latency but it's optional.
[14:02] [00:14:10] Lena Ortiz: okay closing loop — let's recap next steps and action items. Marcus?
[14:10] Marcus Li: recap: 1) bench script + repo (Marcus) 2) Viant shares traffic profile and provisions on-prem cluster (Priya / Tom) 3) Lena sends security and VPC checklist (Lena) 4) run 2-week pilot with shard weighting and soft quotas (all)
[14:31] Priya Shah: sounds good. one last ask — can you simulate a worst-case short-seq storm to make sure our product route stays within p95 200ms?
[14:40] Marcus Li: yes that's part of the bench scenarios — we'll include a ‘‘short-seq storm'' scenario.
[14:46] [00:14:50] Markus Engel: ok i'm comfortable to move forward on the pilot.
[14:52] Lena Ortiz: great, we'll follow up with calendar invites and the repo. thanks everyone.
